svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 3. Module 6 in one table: which observer, which tool
svg.desc: A decision table covering the whole module. Each row names an observer somebody might want to remove, and states which of the tools built across the module actually removes that observer. The network you joined is removed by any tunnel, including one you host yourself. Your own internet provider is removed by any tunnel, at the cost of moving the observation to the provider you chose. A destination building a profile across visits needs Tor rather than a tunnel, because a tunnel gives you one stable address. Wanting to reach a specific country needs a rented server or a commercial provider, and Tor cannot supply it reliably. Wanting a fixed address for an allow list needs a rented server, which is the one case with no substitute. Wanting nobody to hold both halves of your connection needs Tor. An adversary who can watch both ends is removed by nothing in the module. Anything done while signed in is removed by nothing anywhere. A band below states the question the whole module was teaching, which is to name the observer first and then choose, rather than choosing a tool and hoping.
svg.text: Figure 3: Module 6 in One Table. Name the Observer, Then Choose.
Ten lessons, six tools, and one question that decides between them. The question is never which is strongest.
THE OBSERVER YOU WANT TO REMOVE
WHAT ACTUALLY REMOVES IT
AND WHAT THAT COSTS
The network you just joined
a hotel, a cafe, a conference
Any tunnel at all, including one at home
Almost nothing. Lesson 6.1.
Your own internet provider
the one with a billing relationship with you
Any tunnel, or Tor
The observation moves to whoever you
chose instead. It is not removed.
A destination building a profile across visits
recognising you as the same person each time
Tor. A tunnel gives you one stable address
Speed, and Lesson 6.8's list of
behaviours that undo it anyway.
Appearing to be in a particular country
which is a requirement, not a privacy goal
A rented server, or a commercial provider
Tor cannot do this reliably. Exit
selection is not a country picker.
Needing one fixed address that is yours
an allow list at work, a service that rejects shared exits
A rented server. Nothing else supplies it
Lesson 6.6's trust ledger, and an
anonymity set of exactly one.
Anybody holding both halves of your connection
your address and your destination, together
Tor, structurally. Lesson 6.7's Figure 1
Speed, and the caveats in 6.9.
A chain of tunnels approximates it.
An adversary who can watch both ends
a national observer, or a well-placed one
Nothing in this module. The project says so
Lesson 6.9, Figure 1.
Anything you did while signed in
and anything you told them yourself
Nothing, anywhere, ever
Lesson 6.8, Figure 2, first row.
What the module was actually teaching
Read the middle column and notice that no tool appears in every row, and two rows have nothing in them at all. That is the whole argument. There is no
strongest option, because the options are answers to different questions, and the products are all sold as answers to the same one.
So name the observer first. Then look at this table. Then choose, and be able to say what you gave up in exchange.
A recommendation that does not name the observer it removes is not advice. It is a preference, and you cannot check a preference.
Every lesson in this module ended the same way: the measure moved an observation rather than removing one. That is not a disappointment. It is the design.
Knowing exactly where an observation moved to is the difference between using these tools and believing in them.
